checkpoints: Selecting every row from `documents` with no `ORDER BY` and no `LIMIT` forces the full table — id, content, and every embedding vector — to be pulled out of Postgres and shipped over the wire on each retrieval call.

Computing `cosineSimilarity` in application code once per row is an O(n) scan across the entire corpus for every single query, and sorting all of those scored rows in memory before slicing the top 3 wastes work on rows that get thrown away.

This pattern is invisible at a handful of seed documents because the data volume and scan cost are both trivial, but it degrades badly as the corpus grows into the hundreds of thousands of chunks — the LLM call is not the bottleneck, the network transfer and the app-side scan are.

The first-stage fix is to move the nearest-neighbour search into the database itself: query with `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT $2` using pgvector's cosine-distance operator, so Postgres does the ranking and only the top-k rows ever cross the wire.

The similarity-to-score conversion (`1 - distance`) and the `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` filter should still be applied, but only to the k rows the database returns, not to the whole corpus — the app-side `cosineSimilarity` and `parseVectorLiteral` helpers drop out of the request path entirely once the query does the work.

An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat should only be introduced once the exact in-database scan itself becomes the bottleneck at very large scale — it is a second-stage optimization, not an automatic first move.

Adding an ANN index trades exactness for speed: the neighbours returned become approximate rather than guaranteed top-k, so the recall loss versus the latency gain is a judged trade-off rather than a free win.

Verifying the change means measuring p95 query latency before and after at a realistic corpus size, running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the query plan actually uses the index once one exists, checking retrieval quality hasn't silently regressed by comparing approximate results against an exact scan on a sample of queries, and re-running the grounded and fallback end-to-end flows to confirm answers still cite the right chunks.
